name: Fontainebleau
lede: Fontainebleau is a light brownish grey, listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary under the name of the French royal court town and palace.

sections.title: A dictionary name
sections.body: Our library finds the name in Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930, as cited by the ISCC-NBS in 1955 [1]. Measured against the ISCC-NBS categories, the swatch is nearest to light brownish gray, 3.9 units of ΔE2000 away [1]. Why the authors chose the place is undocumented in our sources [1].

sections.title: A court color, perhaps
sections.body:
In the summer of 1775, St Clair relates, King Louis XVI likened a gown of Marie Antoinette's to the color of fleas, a shade between brown, pink and grey, and the court took it up as puce [2]. Lady Spencer wrote that puce was the uniform at Fontainebleau and the only color that could be worn [2].

Nothing we found ties the dictionary entry to that remark, so treat it as context, not origin. Compare [[puce]], [[taupe]] and [[taupe-grey]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This tone appears in 336 paintings in our archive, 1.41 per cent, as photographed [3]. Impressionist paintings carry it in 9 of 140 and Claude Monet in 5 of 50 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [3].

questions.q: In 1775 what did Lady Spencer say was the uniform at Fontainebleau?
True or false: a source we found says Maerz and Paul named this color after the 1775 puce fashion.

openers: In 1775 the court at Fontainebleau was said to wear puce and nothing else.
